pages.title: Today: Continuing Intermediate Representations

pages.text:
[Reminder]
Compilation Strategies and IR Design
High-level Model
• Retain high-level data types: Structs, Arrays, Pointers, Classes
• Retain high-level control constructs
• AST OR 3-address code
• Generally, operate directly on program variables (i.e., no registers)
Mid-level Model
• Retain some high-level data types: Structs, Arrays, Pointers
• Linear 3-address code + CFG
• Distinguish virtual registers from memory
• No low-level architectural details
pages.title: [Reminder] Compilation Strategies and IR Design

pages.text:
[Reminder]
Compilation Strategies and IR Design
Low-level Model
• Linear memory model (no high-level data types)
• Distinguish virtual registers from memory
• Low-level 3-address code + CFG
• Explicit addressing arithmetic
• Expose all low-level architectural details:
Addressing modes, stack frame, calling conventions, data layout
pages.title: [Reminder] Compilation Strategies and IR Design

pages.text:
Intermediate Code Generation
Goal: Translate AST to low-level machine-independent IR
Basic Strategy: Separation of Concerns
• Generate efficient code sequences for individual operations
• Keep it fast and simple: leave most optimizations to later phases
• Provide clean, easy-to-optimize code
• IR forms the basis for code optimization and target code
generation
pages.title: Intermediate Code Generation

pages.text:
Intermediate Code Generation
Goal: Translate AST to low-level machine-independent IR
Mid-level vs. Low-level Model of Compilation
Both models can use a machine-independent IR:
• AST → machine-specific code sequences → target code
• AST → machine-independent code sequences
→ machine-level IR → target code
Key difference: where does “target instruction selection” happen
pages.title: Intermediate Code Generation

pages.text:
Intermediate Code Generation
Goal: Translate AST to low-level (mostly) machine-independent
3-address IR
Assumptions:
• Intermediate language: RISC-like 3-address code (see next slide)
• Intermediate Code Generation (ICG) is independent of target ISA
• Storage layout has been pre-determined
• Infinite number of registers + Frame Pointer (FP)
Q. What values can live in registers?
pages.title: Intermediate Code Generation

pages.title: 3-address code for Lectures (Excerpt)

pages.text:
Why 3-address code?
Easy to show on the slides ☺
Conversion between our 3-address code and CFG is simple:
• Nodes are the sequences of non-jump instructions
• The first statement of each note is annotated with a label
• Edges are conditional or unconditional jumps to the labels
representing the start of the destination nodes
pages.title: Why 3-address code?

pages.text:
Code Generation Strategy
1. Simple bottom-up tree-walk on AST
2. Translation uses only local info: current AST node + children
3. Good (local) code is important!
⇐ Later passes have less semantic information
⇐ E.g., array indexing, boolean expressions, case statements
4. We will discuss important special cases
pages.title: Code Generation Strategy

pages.text:
Code Generation for Expression Trees
Illustrates the tree-walk scheme
• assign a virtual register to each operator
• emit code in postorder traversal of expression tree
Assumptions:
• assume tree reflects precedence, associativity
• assume all operands are integers
• base() and offset() may emit code; base() handles lexical scoping
Support routines
• base( str ) — looks up str in the symbol table and stores the base address for str
in a virtual register; emits the corresponding load.
• offset( str ) — looks up str in the symbol table and stores the offset of str from
its base register in a virtual register; emits the corresponding load
• new_reg_name() — returns a new virtual register name
pages.title: Code Generation for Expression Trees

pages.text:
Code Generation for Expression Trees
Attack strategy:
• If expression is a constant “n”, load the value in a virtual register
• If expression is a variable “x”, load its value into a virtual register
from memory
• If expression is “e1 + e2”,
• Compute the left subexpression e1, store its result in a register “t1”
• Compute the right subexpression e2, store its result in a register “t2”
• Compute the result as “res = t1 + t2

pages.text:
Mixed Type Expressions
Example: x + 4 * 2.3e0
• expression must have a clearly defined meaning
• some languages, e.g., Ocaml forbid mixing; instead: float_of_int(x) +. 4.0 *. 2.3e0
• typically convert to more general type
• complicated, machine dependent code
Typical rule: use conversion table
E.g., x + 4, where Type(x) != Type(4):
1. Type(result) ← Tbl (+, Type(x), Type(4))
2. Convert x to Type(result)
3. Convert 4 to Type(result)
4. Add converted values:
yields Type(result)

pages.text:
Boolean and Relational Expressions
We can define the translation the same way for
• Boolean operators (and, or, xor,...) and
• Relational operators (cmp_LT, cmp_Eq, cmp_GE, ...)
Simple traversal and code generation.
Example: b > 10 and c < 1
pages.title: Boolean and Relational Expressions

pages.text:
Numerical Representation of Booleans
• Assign a value to true, such as 1 (0x00000001) or -1 (0xFFFFFFFF)
• Assign a value to false, such as 0
• Use hardware instructions — and, or, not, xor
• Select values that work with the hardware (0&1 are good, 1&3 are not)
Any optimization possible for languages like C or Java?
• Hint: &&, ||
• Will get back to them later!

pages.text:
Short Circuiting Condition
Terms of a Boolean expression can be evaluated until its value is established. Then, any remaining
terms should not be evaluated.
Examples:
• if (a && foo(b)) ... call to foo() should not be made if a is false.
• if (k > 5 || a[i+1, j, k-1] < 20) ... computing the indices not necessary if k>5
Basic Rules: once value established, stop evaluating
• true or 〈expr〉 is true
• false and 〈expr〉 is false
order of evaluation must be observed
Note: If order of evaluation is unspecified, short-circuiting can be used as an optimization:
reorder by cost and short-circuit
pages.title: Short Circuiting Condition

summary.overview: Phi functions are placed at the first node where multiple paths converge in a control flow graph. Intermediate code generation translates ASTs into 3-address code using a bottom-up tree-walk. Constants are loaded into virtual registers via loadI, while variables are loaded from memory using base addresses and offsets. This process involves assigning a virtual register to each operator and emitting code in postorder traversal of the expression tree.

bullets: The phi function must be placed at the first node where paths converge; if paths from B to B' and another path converge at an earlier node, the phi function belongs at that earlier node.
A phi node is not always required even if multiple values enter a basic block from multiple predecessors.
Announcement: A mini quiz is available on the website and students may want to complete it today.
detail.example: In a diamond structure, you may not necessarily need a phi node even if multiple values enter a basic block.

takeaways.summary: The phi function must be placed at the node where paths converge; if a path from B to B' converges with another path at an earlier node, the phi function belongs at that earlier node.
takeaways.title: Recap: Phi function placement

bullets: To convert an AST expression to 3-address code, the structure of the expression must be analyzed.
Constants are handled by loading the value into a new virtual register using a load immediate instruction.
Variables require loading their value from memory into a virtual register.
For binary operations like E1 + E2, the left sub-expression is computed into register t1 and the right into t2, with the result stored in a new register res.
Virtual registers are assumed to be infinite, so a new register can be created for every new value.
The symbol table is required to find the memory location of a variable.
Q: Can we use the zero register to assign a variable? A: You still need to load the variable from memory first.
detail.example: For the expression y = x + 4, the compiler would first load the constant 4 into a virtual register, then load the variable x from memory into another register, and finally perform an addition of these registers.

takeaways.summary: To convert AST expressions to 3-address code, constants are loaded into virtual registers using loadI, while variables are loaded from memory using loadAO by retrieving the base address and offset from the symbol table.
takeaways.title: AST to 3-address code conversion

takeaways.summary: To load a variable, the base address and offset are retrieved from the symbol table and used with a load instruction to move the value into a register.
takeaways.title: Loading variables from memory
